step1_summary: Chief complaint: New-onset wheeze and shortness of breath

Symptoms: • Began ~2 days ago after cleaning dusty carpet • Gradually worsened; worse at night • Feels short-of-breath and sometimes cannot finish sentences • No chest pain on deep inspiration • No dizziness • Hydrating adequately (4–5 glasses water/day)
Past medical history: Childhood asthma (occasional exertional symptoms as adult); seasonal hay-fever
Medications / allergies: Keeps an old asthma inhaler (likely SABA) but has not used it; no regular meds; no known drug allergies; no OTC antihistamines at home
Family / social history: Not discussed; non-smoker status not explicitly stated; recent dust exposure while house-cleaning
Vital signs / exam: None provided during video call
Labs / imaging: None performed or reported

V: Pulmonary embolism: acute dyspnoea/wheeze can rarely present without pain; needs consideration despite lack of risk factors
Cardiac ischemia (unstable angina/ACS): bronchospasm-equivalent dyspnoea possible but unlikely given age and absence of pain
I: Asthma exacerbation (acute inflammatory airway narrowing) triggered by allergen/irritant
Viral acute bronchitis or early lower-respiratory-tract infection causing reactive airway and wheeze
Atypical pneumonia (e.g., Mycoplasma) – may manifest with wheeze before fever/cough
N: Endobronchial/bronchogenic tumour producing partial obstruction and wheeze (unlikely in 40-y-o but part of ddx)
D: Early COPD / chronic bronchitis (degenerative airway change, especially if smoker)
I2: Drug-induced bronchospasm (e.g., non-selective β-blocker, ACE-inhibitor cough) – no offending meds reported but category noted
Irritant/toxin inhalation (household cleaning chemicals or dust particles)
C: Congenital airway malacia/asthma persisting from childhood
A: Acute allergic (IgE-mediated) reaction to dust mite antigen with lower-airway involvement
Allergic rhinitis with post-nasal drip triggering cough/wheeze
T: Inhaled foreign body (dust/debris) lodging in bronchus causing local wheeze
E: Thyrotoxicosis causing unexplained shortness of breath
Metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis) leading to dyspnoea – no hyperpnoea described

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: History of childhood asthma, typical wheeze pattern, clear temporal relationship to dust exposure, and nocturnal worsening strongly suggest an acute asthma flare.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute allergic reaction / dust-mite hypersensitivity with lower-airway involvement
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dust exposure plus personal history of hay-fever could produce an allergic bronchospasm even in the absence of longstanding asthma.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral upper or lower respiratory tract infection (acute bronchitis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Viral infections can trigger bronchial hyper-reactivity and wheeze; time course fits, but lack of cough, fever, or systemic symptoms makes it less likely than asthma/allergy.
Any acute dyspnoea warrants PE consideration, but absence of risk factors, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, or hemoptysis lowers probability.

supporting_evidence: Personal history: childhood asthma, still owns inhaler
Trigger: onset after heavy dust exposure
Symptoms: expiratory wheeze, nocturnal worsening, short speech phrases
No systemic infection signs (fever, malaise) -> more asthma-like
opposing_evidence: Reports asthma had mostly ‘resolved’; hasn’t needed regular inhalers as adult
No objective peak-flow/vital-sign data to confirm obstruction

supporting_evidence: Immediate dust exposure, known hay-fever/allergic tendencies
No pain, fever, or infection features
opposing_evidence: Persistent for 48 h and worsening rather than rapid resolution typical of mild allergy
No skin rash, eye itch, throat swelling

supporting_evidence: Common cause of new wheeze in adults without active asthma
Two-day progressive course could fit early viral illness
opposing_evidence: No cough, sputum, fever, sore throat, or URI symptoms reported

supporting_evidence: Acute onset dyspnoea can be sole manifestation
opposing_evidence: Age 40 with no mentioned risk factors (immobility, OCP, previous DVT)
No pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, tachycardia, or syncope
Temporal link to dust exposure makes PE less plausible
